title: Year four close
hookLine: law, thought, streams, character, life and language
tomorrow: Year five opens: the sources themselves

cards: A man comes to Hillel with a dare: teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. You may remember him from your first week. The Talmud says Shammai had already sent him away.
Hillel doesn't. He gives him one sentence: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah, he says, and the rest is commentary.

Then two more words, easy to skip past: go and learn. This whole year has been the go and learn: the long commentary that grew around that sentence, the way Jews argue, decide, pray, mourn, celebrate and speak.

teach.b: The year opened with a promise: now, how it works. Here's how it went, in six words. First, law.
The Mishnah and the Talmud, the oral Torah set down, rabbis disagreeing on the record, and the codes that turned argument into practice.
The block closed with the Talmud called a sea: nobody crosses it, but everyone can swim. Second, thought. Maimonides, the physician and philosopher who argued that reason can serve faith.
Then the hidden side: Kabbalah and the Hasidic masters, sparks scattered in the world and a light from creation kept hidden away. Third, streams.
Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist, Renewal, secular and more, each described in its own terms and ranked against none.
Fourth, character, life and language. Mussar taught that traits are built one ordinary day at a time. The life cycle walked from a baby's naming to a wedding canopy to a mourner's kaddish.

And these last weeks, the roots: letters that turn out to be numbers, a break that holds a birth, a name that opens a book, and a single verse you read by yourself. Put them together and you get the year's line.
Judaism isn't only something believed. It's a way of thinking, out loud and in pairs, and a way of living, at the table, the door and the graveside. That's why Hillel didn't stop at one sentence.

how: Jews ask for understanding in the weekday Amidah, in the blessing that closes 'who graciously grants knowledge', and on finishing a tractate of Talmud some hold a siyum, a small celebration of learning completed.

games.q: you're Hillel. a man asks you to teach him the whole Torah while he stands on one foot. what do you do?
o: send him away for mocking the Torah.
give him one sentence, and tell him to go and learn.
tell him to come back in a year.
games.why: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor; the rest is commentary. go and learn.

practice: Let the year pass in front of you: one argument from the Talmud that stuck, one teacher, one trait you worked on, one Hebrew root, just one of each if they come.

The weekday Amidah, the standing prayer, has a blessing that asks God for knowledge, understanding and discernment, and closes by blessing God, who graciously grants knowledge; if you pray, you can say it now from a siddur, in Hebrew or in English.
If you don't, sit with the plain wish behind it: to understand a little more next year than this one.
